PKG_CONFIG='pkg-config'
```

### What did you do?

We run a Go proxy that connects HTTP/2 to an upstream Envoy gateway running nghttp2. The client side of the proxy sends a client-initiated GOAWAY on normal connection teardown — an explicit (*ClientConn).Shutdown, or the transport's own idle/age-based recycling. That part is expected. The problem is the value: sendGoAway sets Last-Stream-ID = cc.nextStreamID, the client's own next stream id, which is always odd.

The below self-contained program drives the real http2.Transport (one request, then Shutdown) against an in-process peer that applies the same rule nghttp2 enforces: a client's GOAWAY Last-Stream-ID must be in the server's stream-id space (server-initiated, i.e. even) or 0. Because the Go client processes no server-initiated streams, 0 is the correct value to send here.

Minimal shape of the trigger:

```
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"net"
	"net/http"

	"golang.org/x/net/http2"
	"golang.org/x/net/http2/hpack"
)

// fakePeer answers one request, then applies the RFC 9113 6.8 / 5.1.1 rule that
// nghttp2 enforces: a client's GOAWAY Last-Stream-ID must be server-initiated
// (even) or 0; an odd (client) id is rejected as PROTOCOL_ERROR.
func fakePeer(nc net.Conn, out chan<- string) {
	defer nc.Close()
	io.ReadFull(nc, make([]byte, len(http2.ClientPreface)))
	fr := http2.NewFramer(nc, nc)
	fr.WriteSettings()
	var hb bytes.Buffer
	enc := hpack.NewEncoder(&hb)
	for {
		f, err := fr.ReadFrame()
		if err != nil {
			return
		}
		switch v := f.(type) {
		case *http2.SettingsFrame:
			if !v.IsAck() {
				fr.WriteSettingsAck()
			}
		case *http2.HeadersFrame:
			hb.Reset()
			enc.WriteField(hpack.HeaderField{Name: ":status", Value: "200"})
			fr.WriteHeaders(http2.HeadersFrameParam{StreamID: v.StreamID,
				BlockFragment: hb.Bytes(), EndHeaders: true, EndStream: true})
		case *http2.GoAwayFrame:
			if id := v.LastStreamID; id != 0 && id%2 == 1 {
				fr.WriteGoAway(0, http2.ErrCodeProtocol, []byte("GOAWAY: invalid last_stream_id"))
				out <- fmt.Sprintf("client GOAWAY Last-Stream-ID=%d (odd) -> PROTOCOL_ERROR", id)
			} else {
				out <- fmt.Sprintf("client GOAWAY Last-Stream-ID=%d -> accepted", id)
			}
			return
		}
	}
}

func main() {
	ln, _ := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")
	defer ln.Close()
	out := make(chan string, 1)
	go func() {
		if nc, err := ln.Accept(); err == nil {
			fakePeer(nc, out)
		}
	}()

	nc, _ := net.Dial("tcp", ln.Addr().String())
	tr := &http2.Transport{}
	cc, _ := tr.NewClientConn(nc)
	req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", "http://"+ln.Addr().String()+"/", nil)
	if resp, err := cc.RoundTrip(req); err == nil {
		fmt.Printf("GET / -> %d (request succeeded)\n", resp.StatusCode)
		resp.Body.Close()
	}
	cc.Shutdown(context.Background()) // client sends the graceful GOAWAY under test
	fmt.Println(<-out)
}
```

### What did you see happen?

The request itself completes fine (GET / -> 200); the problem is the GOAWAY the client sends on shutdown. Its Last-Stream-ID is odd (3), and the conformant peer rejects that frame as a connection PROTOCOL_ERROR. http2: Transport received HEADERS flags=END_STREAM|END_HEADERS stream=1 len=1
GET / -> 200 (request succeeded)
http2: Framer 0xc00019a000: wrote GOAWAY len=8 LastStreamID=3 ErrCode=NO_ERROR Debug=""
http2: Framer 0xc000122000: read GOAWAY len=8 LastStreamID=3 ErrCode=NO_ERROR Debug=""
http2: Framer 0xc000122000: wrote GOAWAY len=38 LastStreamID=0 ErrCode=PROTOCOL_ERROR Debug="GOAWAY: invalid last_stream_id"
http2: Transport readFrame error on conn 0xc0001a2000: (*net.OpError) read tcp 127.0.0.1:62964->127.0.0.1:62963: use of closed network connection
client GOAWAY Last-Stream-ID=3 (odd) -> PROTOCOL_ERROR
```
The three lines that matter: 
- the request succeeds (GET / -> 200); 
- on shutdown the client writes GOAWAY ... LastStreamID=3 (odd); 
- the peer answers GOAWAY ... PROTOCOL_ERROR Debug="GOAWAY: invalid last_stream_id" and closes. 

So the defect is at the connection level: a spec-invalid GOAWAY frame, rejected regardless of what any individual request was doing. The reproducer shows this in isolation (the GET has already finished, so nothing is lost here).

What makes it visible in production is the second-order effect. When this rejection happens during connection recycling, the peer tears the whole connection down (nghttp2 sends its own GOAWAY(PROTOCOL_ERROR) / RST), which kills any other requests still in flight on that same connection. The transport transparently retries idempotent requests on a fresh connection, so those are invisible; a non-idempotent POST that has already written its body can't be retried and surfaces as unexpected EOF -> 5xx. That in-flight race is why the user-visible error rate is low rather than every-connection, but the root cause is the one thing the reproducer shows: the client should not be sending an odd Last-Stream-ID.

This is the parity check nghttp2 enforces — see [the GOAWAY validation](https://github.com/nghttp2/nghttp2/blob/91ad6fdbb42061f6e45c9b67da7b1804958c5877/lib/nghttp2_session.c#L4701-L4707) and [the stream-id parity test](https://github.com/nghttp2/nghttp2/blob/91ad6fdbb42061f6e45c9b67da7b1804958c5877/lib/nghttp2_session.c#L271-L282) it applies (lib/nghttp2_session.c, linked for reference). Envoy's default codec and Apache mod_http2 use nghttp2; nginx, Caddy, and Envoy's newer oghttp2 codec don't check it and accept the same frame.

### What did you expect to see?

The server should accept the graceful GOAWAY and let in-flight streams drain.

Last-Stream-ID is in the receiver's stream-id space — for a GOAWAY sent by a client that means server-initiated (even) streams, so the value must be even or 0 (RFC 9113 §6.8; §5.1.1 for the parity). cc.nextStreamID is odd, so it isn't valid there and nghttp2 rejects it. A default Transport processes no server-initiated streams (push is off), so 0 ("no streams processed", which §6.8 explicitly allows) is correct and accepted by every server we tried:

```
func (cc *ClientConn) sendGoAway() error {
 	cc.mu.Lock()
 	closing := cc.closing
 	cc.closing = true
-	maxStreamID := cc.nextStreamID
+	// Last-Stream-ID must be in the peer's stream-id space: for a client
+	// that's a server-initiated (even) id, or 0. The odd nextStreamID isn't
+	// valid there, so a strict server rejects the GOAWAY as PROTOCOL_ERROR.
+	// The client has no server-initiated streams (push), so 0 is correct.
+	// (If push is ever added, use the last even stream id processed.)
+	maxStreamID := uint32(0)
 	cc.mu.Unlock()
 	...
 }
```

The server-side path (server.go) correctly reports an odd Last-Stream-ID for the client-initiated streams it processed, so it stays as is;  its only the client path that seems wrong.

issue_title: client-go: rest_client metrics lack resource dimensions, making client-side observability difficult
issue_description:
### What happened?

Server-side metrics (e.g. `apiserver_request_duration_seconds`) let you measure latency per verb, resource, group, version, and scope.

However, the client-side metrics exposed by client-go's REST layer use only verb (raw HTTP method) and host as labels. This means:

  - You cannot measure client-side latency per resource. "How long do Pod LIST calls take from the controller's perspective?" is unanswerable.
  - LIST and GET are indistinguishable. The client records the raw HTTP method GET for both. The server distinguishes these as separate verbs.
  - No scope information. You cannot distinguish cluster-scoped from namespace-scoped requests.

Debugging client-side latency is difficult because the metrics lack this information.

We could add resource-aware labels to `rest_client` metrics, similar to what server-side metrics already provide:

1. We could add resource , group, version, and scope labels.
2. We could map HTTP methods to API verbs (GET vs LIST) so verb carries semantic meaning.


Additionally, the recently introduced `A Unified Identity for client-go Components for Enhanced Telemetry` ([xref](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HUNewBqN3lk2DSHJaxKZmmhYgt0SNgp9AqpJTY6cfRM/edit?resourcekey=0-uIvQ3ezUROHa6OKjWZUzcw&tab=t.0#heading=h.qtaj715knfkg))  for client-go components provides a name label that Informers and Reflectors propagate to identify which component initiated a request. This identity could also be passed into rest_client metrics, allowing to correlate API requests back to the specific component that made them.

issue_title: mode-tracker: natural language regex false positives on activation and deactivation
issue_description:
## Problem

The natural language activation/deactivation regexes in `hooks/caveman-mode-tracker.js` (added in #120) match too broadly, causing caveman to activate or deactivate on unrelated prompts.

### False activation

Any prompt containing "start" and "caveman" anywhere triggers activation, even when "caveman" is not the object of the action:

- `"How do I start a caveman fire?"` → activates caveman
- `"I want to start building a caveman-themed game"` → activates caveman
- `"Can you start explaining caveman lifestyle?"` → activates caveman

The root cause is `\b(activate|enable|turn on|start|talk like)\b.*\bcaveman\b` — the `.*` between "start" and "caveman" matches any intervening text.

### Negation ignored

`"don't activate caveman"` still activates. The negative guard checks for `stop|disable|turn off|deactivate` but not `don't`, `do not`, or `no`.

### False deactivation

`/\bnormal mode\b/i` matches without requiring "caveman" anywhere in the prompt:

- `"switch from normal mode to debug mode"` → deactivates caveman
- `"use normal mode for this task"` → deactivates caveman
- `"is this normal mode behavior?"` → deactivates caveman

Users discussing "normal mode" in any unrelated context lose caveman mode silently.

## Evidence

Tested the current regexes against 16 prompts — **9 failed (56% false positive rate)**. The failing cases are all prompts that a real user could plausibly type without intending to change caveman mode.

```
❌ "How do I start a caveman fire?"          → false activation
❌ "I want to start building a caveman game" → false activation
❌ "Can you start explaining caveman life?"  → false activation
❌ "don't activate caveman"                  → activation despite negation
❌ "switch from normal mode to debug mode"   → false deactivation
❌ "use normal mode for this task"           → false deactivation
❌ "is this normal mode behavior?"           → false deactivation
❌ "the normal mode of operation is..."      → false deactivation
```

## Suggested fix

1. Replace broad `start.*caveman` with exact `\bstart caveman\b` so "start a caveman fire" no longer matches
2. Require "caveman" alongside "normal mode" for deactivation: `(/\bnormal mode\b/i.test(prompt) && /\bcaveman\b/i.test(prompt))`
3. Add `don't`, `do not`, `no` to the negative guard

These three changes reduce the test failure rate from 9/16 to 0/19 (expanded test set) while preserving all intended activation phrases from the README.

issue_title: Stack overflow via recursive exception dispatch in bundled Bun on every outbound fetch (Windows 11, v1.18.4 and v1.18.11)
issue_description:
## Summary

On one Windows 11 machine, every `opencode` invocation that performs an outbound network fetch crashes with an unhandled `0xC0000005 ACCESS_VIOLATION`. A full crash dump shows the mechanism: a recursive exception-dispatch loop inside the bundled Bun runtime during the fetch, ending in stack exhaustion (the faulting write lands one page below the bottom of the fetch thread's stack, from a stack-probe stub at `opencode.exe+0x1fc0`).

Local-only code paths (`--version`, `--help`, `auth list`, `serve` until its update check fires) work. Any path that fetches (LLM call in `run`, `models` catalog fetch when uncached, plugin-manifest registry resolution) dies instantly.

## Environment

- Windows 11 Home 10.0.26200, x64
- opencode installed via `npm i -g opencode-ai` (shim execs the self-contained `opencode.exe`)
- Reproduces on v1.18.4 and v1.18.11 identically; the `opencode-windows-x64-baseline` binary is worse (segfaults even on `--version`)
- Reproduces in both Git Bash and PowerShell, from any working directory

## Reproduction

```
opencode run "Reply with exactly the word OK and nothing else."
# exits 139 (Git Bash) / -1073741819 = 0xC0000005 (PowerShell), no output, no log entries
```

`opencode models` crashes the same way until the catalog is cached; once `models.dev` is cached it succeeds because no fetch happens.

## Crash dump analysis

Captured with ProcDump (`-ma -e`), unhandled `C0000005`, full 982 MB dump, parsed with the `minidump` Python library:

```
ExceptionCode:    EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION
ExceptionAddress: 0x00007ff7114b1fc0   (opencode.exe+0x1fc0, early-image stub / stack probe)
Violation:        WRITE of 0x0000001b83600bb8

Faulting thread stack: 0x1b83601000 .. 0x1b84800000
Write target:          0x1b83600bb8   (one page BELOW the stack bottom)
```

The faulting thread's stack scan shows the same ntdll frames repeating over and over (`ntdll+0x3ae640`, `ntdll+0x2e4d4c`, `ntdll+0x3b4c28`, interleaved with two alternating `opencode.exe` frames at `+0x1fd4`/`+0x3da0` and `+0x2828c30`/`+0x383ed47`), i.e. exception dispatch re-entering itself until the stack is gone. Whatever the initial exception is, the handler path re-faults recursively instead of surfacing an error.

## Ruled out on this machine

- Config or state corruption: pristine `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and `XDG_DATA_HOME` still crash
- opencode version: 1.18.4 and 1.18.11 both crash; clean reinstall does not help
- Machine TLS stack: standalone Bun 1.3.14 AND 1.3.9 (`bun -e "await fetch(...)"`) fetch the same URLs fine
- OS changes: no Windows updates installed in the regression window (last good run Jul 21, first dead run later the same day)
- Certificate store: no root/CA certs added in the window
- Winsock LSPs: catalog is all-Microsoft
- Defender: no detections logged for the binary
- WER: no crash reports (the crash bypasses WER entirely; only a debugger catches it)

Possibly related existing reports of bundled-Bun Windows segfaults: #14204, #11339.

## Notes

The full dump is available privately on request (it contains session credentials, so it is not attached). Happy to run instrumented builds or additional captures on the affected machine.

issue_title: hugo mod npm pack emits a publishable, checkout-named package.json
issue_description:
**TL;DR**: the generated `package.json` has no `"private": true` and a checkout-derived `name`, so committed copies are publishable under names sites don't control. Suggested fix: emit `"private": true` and a stable (ideally scoped) default name.

### What version of Hugo are you using (`hugo version`)?

```
hugo v0.165.0-76a5e1880ab46688155b02e99bab9be2a6134492+extended darwin/arm64 BuildDate=2026-08-12T14:26:28Z VendorInfo=gohugoio
```

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?

Yes (transcript below is v0.165.0). The behavior is in master's [package_builder.go](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/master/modules/npm/package_builder.go).

### What happened

`hugo mod npm pack` writes `packages/hugoautogen/package.json` with:

- a **name derived from the checkout directory**, so it varies per clone and can be a registry name the site doesn't control, and
- **no `"private": true`**, npm's do-not-publish guard for internal packages.

The file is regenerated wholesale on each run, so hand-set fields don't survive. From a fresh clone of a repo whose committed copy was hand-normalized:

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/google/docsy-example.git site-a && cd site-a
$ grep -E '"(name|version|private)"' packages/hugoautogen/package.json
  "name": "@docsy/hugoautogen",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "private": true
$ hugo mod npm pack
$ grep -E '"(name|version|private)"' packages/hugoautogen/package.json
  "name": "site-a",
  "version": "0.1.0"
```

A sibling clone of the same repo into `site-b` yields `"name": "site-b"`.

### Why it matters

Sites that commit the generated workspace (e.g. so `npm ci` works without running Hugo first) end up carrying a manifest that npm workspace publishing and common release tools treat as publishable by default: `npm publish --dry-run --workspaces` packs it as `site-a@0.1.0`, while with `"private": true` npm skips the workspace. The name variance also churns the committed manifest, and the lockfile's workspace entry, across differently named checkouts.

### What did you expect

The generated internal workspace is non-publishable (`"private": true`) and has a stable, project-controlled default name rather than the checkout directory's basename. Ideally the default is scoped: a bare name can be claimed on the registry by anyone, a scoped one only by the scope owner.

### Workaround

[docsy-example#487](https://github.com/google/docsy-example/pull/487) follows each pack invocation with a single `npm pkg set` line restoring a scoped name and `private`.

Happy to send a PR for the `private` field (and for the name default, if you have a preference for what it should be).

issue_title: Support SVG parsing in Go picture ingestion
issue_description:
### Problem

The picture pipeline template declares `svg` in its image suffix list, but the Go standalone-image OCR path has no SVG renderer or decoder. `PictureParser` accepts SVG and can package it as an image attachment; this does not provide SVG text extraction or rasterization for OCR.

In #20424, image dispatch validates inputs with `image.DecodeConfig` before running local OCR or optional VLM enhancement. The registered raster decoders cannot read SVG, so an SVG upload returns `image: unknown format` before either path runs. Keeping the existing template suffix list preserves its declaration but does not resolve this parsing gap.

### Reproduction

1. Use the picture ingestion template in the Go backend.
2. Upload a valid SVG containing visible text.
3. Image dispatch rejects it during header decoding, rather than extracting the text. Enabling VLM enhancement does not bypass this validation.

### Expected behavior

Implement SVG parsing in the Go picture ingestion path and align the template declaration with actual runtime support. Evaluate SVG rasterization for the shared OCR pipeline or SVG text extraction, while keeping OCR independent of optional VLM enhancement. Raw SVG support must not be assumed for every vision provider.

Include a self-contained SVG fixture and coverage with VLM disabled and enabled. Apply the image resource limits appropriately to SVG processing and report invalid SVG inputs clearly.

### Scope and related work

Follow-up to #20424, which restores local picture OCR independently of VLM and retains the picture template's existing suffix list. SVG parsing is deferred from that PR. This issue concerns parsing support; image embeddings and retrieval of textless images remain separate work.

issue_title: [Bug]: OpenClaw leaks unreaped hook/tool child processes, causing zombie accumulation and runtime degradation
issue_description: ### Bug type Regression (worked before, now fails) ### Beta release blocker No ### Summary ## Summary OpenClaw appears to leak unreaped child processes from hook/tool execution. Over time these accumulate as zombies under the main `openclaw` process (`openclaw-hooks`, `bash`, `codex`, and occasionally `chrome-headless`). Once enough accumulate, the runtime degrades and can eventually fail to spawn new helper work (`spawn EAGAIN`, `uv_thread_create`, gateway instability, connector silence). Restarting OpenClaw immediately clears the process table and restores service until the leak accumulates again. This is not a single connector failure in our deployment: we have seen the same shape across multiple OpenClaw 2026.6.x versions, and the current affected runtime reports: ```text OpenClaw 2026.6.10 (aa69b12) ``` ## Environment - Runtime: OpenClaw `2026.6.10 (aa69b12)` - OS: Debian 12 GCE VM - OpenClaw launched in Docker with host networking - Workload: - Slack provider enabled - Telegram provider enabled - Codex provider enabled - scheduled/cron work enabled - hook/tool plugins enabled - The issue is most visible on a busy runtime, but the leak pattern is not limited to a single connector. We also see stale `bash` and `codex` children, not only connector-specific workers. ## Symptoms After OpenClaw has been running for hours, process pressure grows steadily. A recent sanitized snapshot: ```text total processes: 336 zombies: 225 dstate: 1 zombie_comm openclaw-hooks 113 zombie_comm bash 108 zombie_comm codex 2 zombie_comm chrome-headless 2 ``` The zombie children are parented by the main `openclaw` process: ```text PID PPID STAT ELAPSED COMMAND 141806 141784 Ssl 20:12:59 openclaw 142413 141806 ZNs 20:07:50 [openclaw-hooks] 143325 141806 ZNs 20:00:41 [openclaw-hooks] 177641 141806 Z 11:33:55 [codex] ... ``` OpenClaw health remains nominal for a while, but the process table continues growing: ```json { "openclaw_reachable": true, "telegram": { "ready": true }, "slack": { "ready": true }, "process_pressure": { "degraded": false, "restart_recommended": false, "process_count": 326, "zombies": 225, "hook_zombies": 113, "d_state": 0, "reasons": [] } } ``` When the leak gets worse, the same runtime reaches degraded/restart territory: ```json { "process_count": 1003, "zombie_processes": 889, "hook_zombie_processes": 798, "d_state_processes": 1, "reasons": [ "hook_zombie_warning", "hook_zombie_degraded" ], "thresholds": { "hook_zombie_warning": 250, "hook_zombie_degraded": 750, "hook_zombie_restart": 800, "total_zombie_restart": 1000 } } ``` In worse incidents we observed downstream runtime failures such as: - `spawn EAGAIN` - `uv_thread_create` - gateway health timeouts / intermittent gateway unavailability - Slack/Telegram messages not being processed - task failures where OpenClaw can no longer start expected helper work Restarting OpenClaw clears the zombies immediately and restores the runtime, which strongly suggests unreaped children rather than external API/network failure. ## Secondary effect: monitoring traffic ramps up On GCE with Google Ops Agent installed, outbound network slowly increases until OpenClaw is restarted. Packet sampling showed the largest outbound flow was the Ops Agent (`otelopscol`) exporting host/process metrics, not OpenAI/Slack/Telegram payloads. This appears to be a consequence of the leak: as the process table grows, per-process metrics export grows. After OpenClaw restart, process count drops and the outbound metric volume falls. ## Expected behavior OpenClaw should reap hook/tool child processes when they exit, including subprocesses created by hook runners and embedded provider/tool helpers. Completed hook/tool invocations should not leave zombie `openclaw-hooks`, `bash`, `codex`, or browser-helper children indefinitely. ## Actual behavior Defunct children remain parented to `openclaw` for many hours, accumulating until runtime health degrades. Restarting OpenClaw is currently the only reliable recovery. ## Why this looks like an OpenClaw process lifecycle bug - Zombies are direct children of the main `openclaw` process. - They survive after the tool/hook work has completed. - They include generic hook/tool child processes (`openclaw-hooks`, `bash`, `codex`, `chrome-headless`), not just one connector-specific worker. - The problem clears only when the parent OpenClaw process is restarted. - We have reproduced the pattern across multiple 2026.6.x versions. ## Related / possibly adjacent issues These may be related but do not seem to cover the same root issue: - #79224 - #77249 - #88870 ## Useful diagnostics we can provide We can provide more sanitized snapshots if useful: - `ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,etime,comm,args` - OpenClaw gateway logs around the degradation window - process-pressure watcher summaries - packet-header-only traffic samples showing Ops Agent traffic growing with process count ### Steps to reproduce I do not yet have a minimal synthetic reproducer, but the issue is reproducible in a long-running OpenClaw runtime under connector/tool load: 1. Run OpenClaw 2026.6.x on a Linux VM with gateway enabled. 2. Configure Slack and/or Telegram connectors. 3. Enable hook/tool execution paths that spawn child processes, including connector ingestion, scheduled/cron tasks, and normal agent tool calls. 4. Let the runtime process real connector traffic for several hours without restarting the OpenClaw container. 5. Periodically inspect the OpenClaw process tree with `ps`, `pstree`, or equivalent host process metrics. Observed result: child processes created by OpenClaw/tool/hook execution become zombies and remain parented under the OpenClaw process instead of being reaped. The zombie count grows over time, eventually causing process/thread exhaustion and runtime degradation. ### Expected behavior OpenClaw should reap all completed hook/tool child processes promptly. A long-running gateway/runtime should keep a stable process count under normal connector and tool usage. Completed child processes should not accumulate as zombies, and the runtime should not degrade into `spawn EAGAIN`, `uv_thread_create`, gateway timeouts, connector silence, or required container restarts. If a tool or hook subprocess cannot be reaped normally, OpenClaw should detect it, log a bounded diagnostic, clean it up or quarantine it, and continue operating without unbounded zombie/process growth. ### Actual behavior Completed hook/tool child processes remain as zombies parented under the OpenClaw runtime process. Over time the zombie count and total process count grow without being cleaned up. Once enough zombies accumulate, the runtime begins failing unrelated operations because the host/container hits process or thread limits. Observed failures include: - `spawn EAGAIN` - `uv_thread_create` failures from Node - gateway requests timing out or becoming intermittently unavailable - Slack/Telegram connectors appearing configured but no longer responding reliably - normal shell commands such as `ps` or `ulimit` failing with `Resource temporarily unavailable` - runtime recovery requiring an OpenClaw/container restart, after which the zombie count drops and service resumes This appears to be cumulative: the runtime can work normally for hours, then progressively degrades as unreaped child processes build up. ### OpenClaw version 2026.06.10 ### Operating system Debian 12 on Google Compute Engine VM ### Install method Docker image deployed by provisioning automation/Terraform on a GCE VM. OpenClaw runs as a long-lived container with host networking, managed by systemd. ### Model GPT-5.5 on Codex subscription ### Provider / routing chain User message arrives through Slack or Telegram connector, then through the local OpenClaw gateway/runtime on the VM, then to the configured OpenAI/Codex provider path used by the OpenClaw agent. The issue appears before or around local hook/tool/process execution and is not specific to one upstream model response path. ### Additional provider/model setup details The affected runtime uses OpenClaw gateway mode with connector channels enabled for Slack and Telegram. The agent is configured with OpenAI/Codex auth for main turns, plus local tools/hooks and scheduled jobs. The zombie accumulation appears tied to local subprocess lifecycle management for hooks/tools/connectors, not to API key validity or model selection. We have observed it across multiple OpenClaw 2026.6.x versions and after changing VM size. Restarting the OpenClaw container clears the accumulated zombies temporarily, but they start accumulating again during normal connector/tool activity. No API keys, tokens, or secrets are included here. ### Logs ```shell # One example: OpenClaw process pressure: source host_proc hook zombies: 800+ total zombies: 800+ total processes: 900+ D-state processes: 1 restart recommended # Another one: OpenClaw process pressure: hook zombies: ~4000 total zombies: ~4000 process/thread exhaustion symptoms present ``` ### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence ### Impact and severity Affects users - needed to create a separate watcher that restarts OpenClaw every few hours ### Additional information Did not notice this issue before 2026.6.8 (maybe should say before 2026.6.X)

issue_title: think: "low"/"medium"/"high" ignored for Qwen3.8 GGUF whose chat template supports reasoning_effort (always runs at template default xhigh)
issue_description:
### What is the issue?

For a Qwen3.8 27B GGUF whose embedded chat template supports graded reasoning effort, `/api/chat` accepts `think: "low"`, `"medium"` and `"high"` but behaves the same as `think: true`. Only `think: false` changes anything.

The template in the GGUF (`tokenizer.chat_template`) contains:

```jinja
{%- set resolved_reasoning_effort = reasoning_effort|default('xhigh') %}
{%- if resolved_reasoning_effort not in ('xhigh', 'medium', 'low') %}
   {{- raise_exception('Unexpected reasoning effort ' ~ reasoning_effort ~ '. Supported types are xhigh (default), medium, and low.') }}
```

So the model has native low/medium effort, but the level from `think` doesn't seem to reach the template. Every request runs at the template default, `xhigh`.

Measurements: same model and prompt ("Say hi in 3 words."), `num_predict` 400:

| `think` | generated tokens | time |
|---|---|---|
| `true` | 99 | 43.2 s |
| `"low"` | 89 | 21.4 s |
| `"high"` | 96 | 18.7 s |
| `false` | 4 | 3.7 s |

(The first call included warm-up.) In agent use, `think: "low"` produced 1,809 thinking tokens for a one-line chat message.

Rendering the same template myself with `reasoning_effort="low"` and sending it with `raw: true` to `/api/generate` gives much shorter thinking (10–66 tokens on similar prompts).

**Expected:** for models whose template supports `reasoning_effort` (or `enable_thinking` plus effort), map `think: "low" | "medium" | "high"` to that template variable, as is done for gpt-oss. Otherwise, return an error or warning saying levels aren't supported for this model, instead of silently treating them as `true`.

### Relevant log output

```shell
N/A (behavioral)
```

### OS

Linux (Debian 13)

### GPU

Nvidia (RTX 3050 8 GB, partial CPU offload)

### CPU

AMD

### Ollama version

0.35.0
